title: Extra Virgin Olive Oil Versus Olive Oil on Health Status
official: Multidisciplinary Approach to Characterizing the Metabolic Fingerprint of Culinary-processed Extra Virgin Olive Oil Versus Olive Oil (UNIVO)
summary: Extra virgin olive oil (EVOO) is a key component of the Mediterranean diet and is widely recognized for its beneficial health effects, largely attributed to its high content of bioactive compounds such as polyphenols and monounsaturated fatty acids. However, in real-life conditions, olive oil is frequently consumed after culinary processing (e.g., frying, baking), which may alter its chemical composition and biological properties. In contrast, regular olive oil (OO) undergoes industrial processing that reduces its content of bioactive compounds and may generate potentially harmful substances. Despite increasing evidence supporting the health benefits of EVOO, there is a lack of clinical studies evaluating how culinary processing influences the metabolic response to different types of olive oil in humans. Furthermore, no specific metabolic biomarkers are currently available to distinguish the intake of thermally processed EVOO versus OO. Therefore, this study aims to identify and validate a distinctive metabolic fingerprint associated with the consumption of EVOO and OO after cooking, using a randomized, controlled, crossover, dose-response clinical trial in healthy adults. The findings will contribute to a better understanding of the health implications of culinary practices involving olive oil and support evidence-based dietary recommendations.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Healthy adults (defined as an individual with no chronic or acute pathologies and whose biochemical parameters are within a normal range)
* Body mass index: \<27 kg/m2
* Age: ≥18 to 70 years old.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Smokers
* Presence of cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, or metabolic disease
* Mental disorders (e.g., depression, dementia, autism, etc.)
* Cardiovascular abnormalities in cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose, etc.
* Regular use of antibiotics, vitamin supplements, corticosteroids, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
* Adherence to restrictive diets or dietary patterns that may interfere with lipid metabolism
* Excessive alcohol consumption (\>30 grams/day for men and \>20 grams/day for women)
* Pregnancy or breastfeeding
* Participation in another ongoing research study
* Intolerance or allergy to olive oil or wheat
